Micah comes from the countryside. Like Amos, he denounces the powerful who seize the fields of others, the judges who accept bribes, the prophets who preach for money. He announces the fall of Samaria, and even that of Jerusalem. A century later, elders will recall that this prophecy led King Hezekiah to repentance (Jeremiah 26:18–19).

But Micah also announces a ruler who will come from Bethlehem, "little among the thousands of Judah" (Micah 5:1). And he sums up all of God's will in one famous sentence: practice justice, love mercy, and walk humbly with your God (Micah 6:8).
plan: The Coming Kingdom and the Ruler from Bethlehem
themes: Dieu demande justice, miséricorde et humilité (Michée 6:8).
Malheur aux responsables qui exploitent ceux qu'ils devraient protéger.
Le libérateur viendra d'un petit village (Michée 5:1).
Quel Dieu est semblable à toi, qui pardonnes l'iniquité ? (Michée 7:18)

versets.t: But you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, though you are little among the thousands of Judah, yet out of you shall come forth to Me the One to be Ruler in Israel, whose goings forth are from of old, from everlasting.
He has shown you, O man, what is good; and what does the Lord require of you but to do justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?
Who is a God like You, pardoning iniquity and passing over the transgression of the remnant of His heritage? He does not retain His anger forever, because He delights in mercy.

33.christ: When the magi ask where the King of the Jews is to be born, the experts in the law quote Micah: "In Bethlehem of Judea" (Matthew 2:5). He who is born there has an origin that "is from of old, from everlasting" (Micah 5:1).

34.resume: A century after Nineveh's repentance in Jonah's time, Assyria has become cruel again. Nahum announces the fall of its capital: God does not leave evil unpunished.
34.auteur: Nahum d'Elkosch (Nahum 1:1), dont on ne sait rien d'autre.
34.date: Between the conquest of the Egyptian city of Thebes, called No-Amon (Nahum 3:8), in 663 B.C., and the fall of Nineveh in 612 B.C.
34.destinataires: Judah, long oppressed by Assyria; and Nineveh itself.
34.contexte:
Assyria crushed the northern kingdom in 722 B.C. and humiliated Judah. Nahum announces the fall of Nineveh, considered impregnable. For Judah, this is good news: "Behold on the mountains the feet of him who brings good tidings, who proclaims peace!" (Nahum 2:1).

Nineveh will indeed fall in 612 B.C. under the blows of the Babylonians and the Medes. The book reminds us of two truths that go together: the Lord is slow to anger, but He will not leave the guilty unpunished (Nahum 1:3); and He is good, a refuge in the day of distress (Nahum 1:7).
themes: Dieu est patient, mais il ne laisse pas le mal impuni (Nahum 1:3).
L'Éternel est bon, un refuge au jour de la détresse (Nahum 1:7).
Aucun empire, si puissant soit-il, n'échappe à Dieu.

versets.t: The Lord is slow to anger and great in power, and will not at all acquit the wicked. The Lord has His way in the whirlwind and in the storm, and the clouds are the dust of His feet.
The Lord is good, a stronghold in the day of trouble; and He knows those who trust in Him.

Behold on the mountains the feet of him who brings good tidings, who proclaims peace! Keep your appointed feasts, O Judah; perform your vows! For the wicked one shall no more pass through you; he is utterly cut off.

34.christ: Paul uses the image of the messenger's feet for those who announce the Gospel: "How beautiful are the feet of those who preach the gospel of peace" (Romans 10:15). The fall of Nineveh announces God's ultimate victory over every power that oppresses mankind.

35.accroche: The Righteous Will Live by Faith
35.resume: Habakkuk dares to question God: why allow violence to triumph? And why use the Babylonians, who are even more wicked? God's answer leads him from complaint to praise.
35.auteur: Habacuc, le prophète (Habacuc 1:1). On ne sait rien d'autre de lui.
35.date: Shortly before the Babylonian invasion, when God announces: "I am raising up the Chaldeans" (Habakkuk 1:6), around 609–598 B.C.
35.destinataires: Judah, and all those who wrestle with God's apparent silence.
35.contexte:
Habakkuk doesn't begin by speaking to the people—he speaks to God. Why do you let violence and injustice triumph in Judah? God answers that he is raising up the Chaldeans, the Babylonians, to punish. Habakkuk is even more troubled: how can God use a people who are even more wicked?

God answers that the proud will fall, "but the righteous will live by his faith" (Habakkuk 2:4). The book ends with a song of absolute trust: even if the fig tree doesn't blossom and the barns are empty, "yet I will rejoice in the Lord" (Habakkuk 3:18).
plan: The answer: the righteous will live by his faith
themes: On peut porter ses questions à Dieu, et attendre sa réponse (Habacuc 2:1).
Le juste vit en faisant confiance à Dieu (Habacuc 2:4).
La terre sera remplie de la connaissance de sa gloire (Habacuc 2:14).
Se réjouir en Dieu quand tout manque (Habacuc 3:18).

versets.t: Behold, his soul is puffed up; it is not upright within him. But the righteous shall live by his faith.
For the earth will be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the Lord, as the waters cover the sea.

Though the fig tree should not blossom, nor fruit be on the vines, the produce of the olive tree fail and the fields yield no food, the flock be cut off from the fold and there be no herd in the stalls, yet I will rejoice in the Lord; I will take joy in the God of my salvation.

35.christ: "The righteous will live by faith" is quoted three times in the New Testament, first by Paul (Romans 1:17). This verse is what shook Luther and launched the Reformation: you are declared righteous before God by faith in Jesus Christ, not by your works.

36.accroche: The God Who Rejoices in His People
36.resume: Under the young King Josiah, Zephaniah announces the "day of the Lord," a day of wrath for Judah and the nations. But it ends with God's joy in the midst of a purified people.
36.auteur: Sophonie, fils de Cuschi (Sophonie 1:1). Sa généalogie remonte à un Ézéchias, peut-être le roi : Sophonie aurait alors été de sang royal.
36.date: Under Josiah (640–609 BC), probably before his great reform in 622 BC.
36.destinataires: Judah and Jerusalem, after the long idolatrous reign of Manasseh.
36.contexte:
Zephaniah preaches under the young King Josiah, after decades of idolatry under Manasseh. He announces the "day of the Lord," a day of wrath that will strike Judah and all nations. This message may have helped prepare the way for Josiah's reform.

He calls the humble to seek the Lord (Zephaniah 2:3). Then the book ends with one of the most beautiful promises in the Bible: the Lord in the midst of His people "like a mighty Savior," who will make them His greatest joy (Zephaniah 3:17).
plan: The Day of the Lord Upon Judah
A Call to Repentance and Judgment of the Nations
themes: Dieu viendra juger le mal, en Juda comme ailleurs.
Cherchez l'Éternel, vous tous, humbles du pays (Sophonie 2:3).
Dieu garde un peuple humble et petit qui se confie en lui (Sophonie 3:12).
Dieu se réjouit de son peuple avec allégresse (Sophonie 3:17).

versets.t: Seek the Lord, all you humble of the earth, Who practice His ordinances! Seek righteousness, seek humility! Perhaps you will be hidden in the day of the Lord's wrath.
The Lord your God is in your midst, like a mighty Savior; He will rejoice over you with joy; He will rest in His love; He will exult over you with singing.

36.christ: Zephaniah announces that God will be "in your midst, like a mighty Savior" (Zephaniah 3:17). In Jesus, Emmanuel, "God with us," the Savior has come to dwell in the midst of His people.

37.resume: The temple still lies in ruins, eighteen years after the return from exile. Haggai shakes the people: everyone is taking care of their own house while neglecting God's. In twenty-three days, the project is back on track.
37.auteur: Aggée, le prophète (Aggée 1:1). On ne sait rien d'autre de lui ; il est cité avec Zacharie dans le livre d'Esdras.
37.date: In 520 BC, the second year of King Darius (Haggai 1:1). His four messages span less than four months.
37.destinataires: Governor Zerubbabel, High Priest Joshua, and the people who had returned from exile.
37.contexte:
The temple's foundations were laid shortly after the return, but the project has been stalled for years. Everyone is busy with their own paneled houses while God's house remains in ruins (Haggai 1:4). The result: they sow much but reap little.

Haggai, together with Zechariah, stirs the people and their leaders: twenty-three days after his first message, the work resumes (Haggai 1:15). To the elders who find this temple quite poor compared to Solomon's, God promises: "The glory of this latter house will be greater than the glory of the former" (Haggai 2:9).
themes: Est-ce le temps d'habiter vos maisons lambrissées, quand celle de Dieu est en ruine ? (Aggée 1:4)
Fortifiez-vous et travaillez, car je suis avec vous (Aggée 2:4).
Ce qui compte n'est pas la splendeur du bâtiment mais la présence de Dieu.
Dieu promet une gloire plus grande que celle du passé (Aggée 2:9).

versets.t: Now be strong, Zerubbabel, says the Lord. Be strong, Joshua son of Jehozadak, the high priest. Be strong, all you people of the land, says the Lord. And work! For I am with you, declares the Lord Almighty.
The glory of this latter house will be greater than the glory of the former house, says the Lord Almighty. And in this place I will grant peace, declares the Lord Almighty.

37.christ: God promises to keep Zerubbabel, descendant of David, "as a signet ring" (Haggai 2:23): the royal line continues, and Zerubbabel appears in the genealogy of Jesus (Matthew 1:12). It is Jesus who will enter this second temple, giving it a glory that Solomon's temple never possessed.

38.resume: A contemporary of Haggai, Zechariah encourages the returned exiles to complete the temple through eight nighttime visions, then looks further ahead: a humble king riding on a donkey, a rejected shepherd, a pierced one who will be mourned.
38.auteur: Zacharie, fils de Bérékia, fils d'Iddo (Zacharie 1:1), sacrificateur et prophète.
38.date: His ministry begins in 520 BC, in the second year of Darius (Zechariah 1:1). Chapters 9–14 likely date from a later period.
38.destinataires: The Jews who had returned from exile in Jerusalem.
plan: The King who comes and the rejected shepherd
themes: L'œuvre de Dieu s'accomplit par son Esprit, pas par la force humaine (Zacharie 4:6).
Revenez à moi, et je reviendrai à vous (Zacharie 1:3).
Un roi humble, un berger rejeté, un transpercé : le portrait du Messie se dessine.
L'Éternel sera roi de toute la terre (Zacharie 14:9).

versets.t: Therefore tell them, 'This is what the Lord Almighty says:
Then he said to me,
Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion! Shout, daughter of Jerusalem! See, your king comes to you, righteous and victorious, lowly and riding on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey.

38.christ: The king riding on a donkey (Zechariah 9:9) enters Jerusalem on Palm Sunday (Matthew 21:5). The thirty pieces of silver (Zechariah 11:12) foreshadow the price of Judas's betrayal. And

39.resume: The temple is rebuilt, but fervor has waned. In a sharp dialogue with His people, God denounces neglected worship and announces the messenger who will prepare the way for the Lord's coming.
39.auteur: Malachie, dont le nom signifie « mon messager ». On ne sait rien d'autre de lui.
39.date: Around 430 BC, in the time of Nehemiah: the same problems appear there (neglected tithes, marriages with idolatrous women, lax priests).
39.destinataires: The Jews returned from exile, particularly the priests.
39.contexte:
The priests offer lame or sick animals, tithes are no longer brought, wives are easily divorced. The people even doubt God's love: "How have you loved us?" (Malachi 1:2).

The book is structured as a dialogue: God makes a claim, the people object, God responds. Malachi announces that the Lord will suddenly enter His temple, preceded by a messenger (Malachi 3:1), and promises to send the prophet Elijah before the great day of the Lord (Malachi 4:5). After him, the voice of the prophets falls silent for approximately four centuries.
plan: Rebukes to the Priests and the People
The Sun of Righteousness and Elijah
themes: Dieu commence par rappeler son amour (Malachie 1:2).
Dieu mérite le meilleur, pas les restes.
Dieu hait la répudiation et appelle à la fidélité conjugale (Malachie 2:16).
Apportez toutes les dîmes, et mettez Dieu à l'épreuve (Malachie 3:10).

versets.t: Behold, I send My messenger, and he will prepare the way before Me. And the Lord, whom you seek, will suddenly come to His temple, even the Messenger of the covenant, in whom you delight. Behold, He is coming, says the Lord of hosts.
For I am the Lord, I do not change; therefore you are not consumed, O sons of Jacob.

Bring the whole tithe into the storehouse, that there may be food in My house. Test Me now in this, says the Lord of hosts, and see if I will not open to you the windows of heaven and pour out a blessing until there is no room to receive it.

Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and dreadful day of the Lord comes. And he will turn the hearts of the fathers to the children, and the hearts of the children to their fathers, lest I come and strike the earth with a curse.

39.christ: Jesus declares that John the Baptist is the messenger announced by Malachi (Matthew 11:10), and that he is "the Elijah who was to come" (Matthew 11:14). The last page of the Old Testament thus opens directly onto the first page of the New.

40.resume: Matthew shows that Jesus is the Messiah announced by the prophets, the son of David who inaugurates the kingdom of heaven. His teaching is organized into five major discourses, including the Sermon on the Mount.
40.auteur: Le livre ne porte pas de signature. Dès le IIe siècle, la tradition l'attribue à l'apôtre Matthieu, le collecteur d'impôts appelé par Jésus (Matthieu 9:9), aussi nommé Lévi.
40.date: Probably between AD 60 and 80; the exact date is debated.
40.destinataires: Primarily Jewish Christians familiar with Scripture and the customs of Israel.
40.contexte:
Matthew opens the New Testament with a genealogy: Jesus is "the son of David, the son of Abraham" (Matthew 1:1), the heir of all the promises. The entire book aims to show that he fulfills Scripture; the phrase "so that what the Lord had spoken through the prophet might be fulfilled" returns like a refrain (Matthew 1:22).

Jesus' teaching is organized into five major discourses, beginning with the Sermon on the Mount. The central theme is "the kingdom of heaven," an expression unique to Matthew. The book ends with the sending of the disciples to all nations, with a promise: "I am with you always, to the very end of the age" (Matthew 28:20).
plan: Birth and childhood of the King
Miracles and the sending of the Twelve
Opposition and the parables of the kingdom
On the way to the cross
themes: Jésus accomplit la Loi et les prophètes, il ne les abolit pas (Matthieu 5:17).
Dieu commence à régner là où Jésus est accueilli (Matthieu 6:33).
Une justice qui vient du cœur et dépasse celle des pharisiens (Matthieu 5:20).
Faire de toutes les nations des disciples (Matthieu 28:19).

versets.t: Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.
But seek first his kingdom and his righteousness, and all these things will be given to you as well.
Come to me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest.
Simon Peter answered, "You are the Messiah, the Son of the living God."

Therefore go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, and teaching them to obey everything I have commanded you. And surely I am with you always, to the very end of the age.

40.christ: Matthew presents Jesus as the King-Messiah, descendant of David, and as Emmanuel, "God with us" (Matthew 1:23). The book opens with this promise and closes with the same: "I am with you always" (Matthew 28:20).

41.accroche: The Son of God Who Came to Serve
41.resume: The shortest and fastest of the Gospels. Jesus acts, heals, teaches with authority, then walks resolutely toward the cross, where a Roman centurion recognizes in him the Son of God.
41.auteur: Jean surnommé Marc (Actes 12:12), compagnon de Paul et de Barnabas, puis de Pierre, qui l'appelle « mon fils » (1 Pierre 5:13). Selon un témoignage du IIe siècle, Marc a mis par écrit la prédication de Pierre.
41.date: Generally dated between A.D. 55 and 70. Many scholars consider it the first Gospel written.
41.destinataires: Probably written for Christians in Rome of pagan origin: Mark explains Jewish customs (Mark 7:3-4) and translates Aramaic words.
41.contexte:
No birth narrative: from the very first verse, the tone is set—"The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God" (Mark 1:1). The narrative is lively, the word "immediately" appears repeatedly. Jesus heals, casts out demons, teaches with authority, yet he often demands silence about his identity.

Midway through the book, Peter confesses: "You are the Christ" (Mark 8:29). From that point on, everything turns toward Jerusalem and the cross, and it is a Roman centurion, a Gentile, who recognizes at the foot of the cross: "Truly this man was the Son of God" (Mark 15:39).
plan: John the Baptist, the baptism, and the first disciples
themes: Il est venu pour servir et donner sa vie (Marc 10:45).
Sur la maladie, les démons, la tempête et même le péché (Marc 2:10).
La question traverse le livre, jusqu'à la confession du centenier (Marc 15:39).
Renoncer à soi-même, se charger de sa croix et le suivre (Marc 8:34).

versets.t: And saying, "The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand. Repent, and believe in the gospel."
When He had called the people to Himself, with His disciples also, He said to them, "Whoever desires to come after Me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow Me."
For even the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give His life a ransom for many.
He said to them, "Do not be alarmed. You seek Jesus of Nazareth, who was crucified. He is risen! He is not here. See the place where they laid Him."

41.christ: Mark sums up Jesus' mission in one sentence: "The Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give His life a ransom for many" (Mark 10:45).

42.resume: Luke investigated to write an orderly account of Jesus' life. He has a special eye for the poor, women, strangers, and sinners: Jesus came to seek what was lost.
42.auteur: Luc, le médecin bien-aimé (Colossiens 4:14), compagnon de voyage de Paul. Il est aussi l'auteur des Actes, adressés au même Théophile (Actes 1:1).
42.date: Probably between A.D. 60 and 80, before the book of Acts.
42.destinataires: A certain Theophilus (Luke 1:3), and through him readers of Greek culture.
42.contexte:
Luke was not a witness to Jesus' life. He conducted an investigation, "having traced the course of all things accurately from the beginning" (Luke 1:3), to write an orderly account of them. This is the longest Gospel, and the most carefully crafted in literary style.

Luke has a special eye for those left behind: the poor, women, Samaritans, tax collectors, sinners. He alone reports the parables of the good Samaritan and the prodigal son, and the encounter with Zacchaeus. The heart of Jesus' mission is stated this way: "the Son of Man came to seek and to save that which was lost" (Luke 19:10).
themes: Une bonne nouvelle qui sera pour tout le peuple le sujet d'une grande joie (Luc 2:10).
La joie du ciel pour un seul pécheur qui se repent (Luc 15:7).
Luc montre souvent Jésus en prière, avant chaque grande étape (Luc 6:12).
Jésus agit par la puissance de l'Esprit (Luc 4:18).

versets.t: Today in the city of David there has been born to you a Savior, who is Christ the Lord.
In the same way, I tell you, there will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous persons who need no repentance.
For the Son of Man came to seek and to save that which was lost.
Jesus said to him, "I say to you, today you shall be with Me in paradise."

42.christ: Luke shows in Jesus the Savior announced from the night of Christmas: "there has been born to you a Savior, who is Christ the Lord" (Luke 2:11). Even on the cross, He continues to save, promising paradise to a repentant criminal (Luke 23:43).

43.resume: John's Gospel begins before creation: Jesus is the eternal Word made flesh. Through seven signs and seven "I am" declarations, he leads you to believe in him and have life.
43.auteur: « Le disciple que Jésus aimait » (Jean 21:20), celui qui a mis ces choses par écrit (Jean 21:24) ; la tradition l'identifie à l'apôtre Jean, fils de Zébédée.
43.date: Generally around AD 90; according to tradition, in Ephesus.
43.destinataires: Believers to strengthen and seekers to lead to faith.
43.contexte:
John doesn't begin at Bethlehem or the Jordan, but before creation: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God" (John 1:1). His Gospel is very different from the three others: few parables, but long dialogues, and chosen "signs," from water turned to wine to the raising of Lazarus.

Jesus presents himself through seven "I am" declarations: the bread of life, the light of the world, the door, the good shepherd, the resurrection and the life, the way, the truth and the life, the true vine. John himself tells why he wrote: "that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may have life in His name" (John 20:31).
themes: Croire en Jésus, c'est recevoir la vie éternelle (Jean 3:16).
Celui qui a vu Jésus a vu le Père (Jean 14:9).
Un commandement nouveau : aimez-vous comme je vous ai aimés (Jean 13:34).
Jésus promet l'Esprit, qui conduira dans toute la vérité (Jean 16:13).

versets.t: And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we beheld His glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father, full of grace and truth.
For God so loved the world that He gave His only begotten Son, that whoever believes in Him should not perish but have everlasting life.
Jesus said to her, "I am the resurrection and the life. He who believes in Me, though he may die, he shall live..."
Jesus said to him, "I am the way, the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through Me."
But these are written that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may have life in His name.

43.christ: All of John's Gospel is centered on Jesus' identity: the Word made flesh, the only begotten Son who reveals the Father (John 1:18). It culminates in Thomas's confession before the Risen One: "My Lord and my God!" (John 20:28).

44.accroche: To the Ends of the Earth
44.resume: After the Ascension, the Holy Spirit descends upon the disciples. The Gospel spreads from Jerusalem, reaches Samaria, then the pagan world, carried by Peter and then by Paul, all the way to Rome.
44.auteur: Luc, qui en fait la suite de son Évangile (Actes 1:1). Dans plusieurs passages, le récit passe au « nous » : Luc voyageait alors avec Paul (Actes 16:10).
44.date: The account spans from the Ascension (around AD 30) to Paul's two years in Rome (around AD 60–62). It was likely written between AD 62 and 80.
44.destinataires: Theophilus, as with the Gospel of Luke, and through him the entire Church.
44.contexte:
Before ascending to heaven, Jesus gives the outline of the book: "you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth" (Acts 1:8). At Pentecost, the Holy Spirit descends, Peter preaches, and about three thousand people are baptized.

The first part follows Peter and the Jerusalem church, then the scattering after Stephen's martyrdom. A persecutor, Saul of Tarsus, is turned around on the Damascus road. The second part follows Paul's missionary journeys through Asia Minor and Greece, until his arrival in Rome as a prisoner, where he proclaims the kingdom of God "quite openly and without hindrance" (Acts 28:31).
plan: The First Missionary Journey and the Jerusalem Council
The Second and Third Missionary Journeys
themes: La puissance de l'Esprit fait des disciples des témoins (Actes 1:8).
Enseignement, communion fraternelle, fraction du pain et prières (Actes 2:42).
Il n'y a de salut en aucun autre qu'en Jésus (Actes 4:12).
Juifs, Samaritains, païens : tous sont appelés (Actes 10:34-35).

versets.t: But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth.
And they devoted themselves to the apostles' teaching and the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and the prayers.
And there is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved.
And they said, "Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household."

44.christ: Luke says his first book recounted "all that Jesus began to do and teach" (Acts 1:1): Acts tells what the risen Christ continues to do through his Spirit and his Church.

45.resume: In his most structured letter, Paul exposes the Gospel: all have sinned, all can be freely declared righteous by faith in Jesus Christ, and live a new life through the Spirit.
45.auteur: L'apôtre Paul (Romains 1:1), qui la dicte à Tertius (Romains 16:22).
45.date: Around 57 A.D., probably from Corinth, at the end of his third missionary journey, before bringing to Jerusalem the collection for the poor (Romans 15:25).
45.destinataires: The Church in Rome, made up of believers from both Jewish and pagan backgrounds, whom Paul had never yet visited.
45.contexte:
Paul did not found the Church in Rome, but he hopes to stop there on his way to Spain (Romans 15:24). He writes to them, therefore, the most complete exposition of the Gospel that he preaches: all, both Jews and Gentiles, have sinned and are deprived of the glory of God; all can be freely justified by his grace (Romans 3:23-24).

He then explains the new life through the Spirit, the place of Israel in God's plan, and then the very practical consequences of the Gospel in the life of the Church. This letter shaped history: Augustine, Luther, and Wesley were deeply moved by reading it.
plan: New life in Christ and through the Spirit
themes: Dieu déclare juste celui qui croit en Jésus (Romains 3:24).
Le salut est un don gratuit, non un salaire (Romains 6:23).
Il n'y a aucune condamnation pour ceux qui sont en Jésus-Christ (Romains 8:1).
Ne vous conformez pas au siècle présent, mais soyez transformés (Romains 12:2).

versets.t: For I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ, for it is the power of God to salvation for everyone who believes, for the Jew first and also for the Greek.
For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, being justified freely by His grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.
But God demonstrates His own love toward us, in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
And we know that all things work together for good to those who love God, to those who are called according to His purpose.
And do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, that you may prove what is that good and acceptable and perfect will of God.

45.christ: Romans places the cross at the center: "But God demonstrates His own love toward us, in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us" (Romans 5:8). Through faith and baptism, the believer is united to His death and resurrection (Romans 6:4).

46.accroche: A Church Full of Gifts—and Problems
46.resume: Paul addresses divisions, disorder, and questions facing a young, vibrant but troubled Church: marriage, freedom, worship, spiritual gifts, resurrection—with love at the center.
46.date: Around A.D. 55, written from Ephesus (1 Corinthians 16:8).
46.destinataires: The Church of Corinth, founded by Paul during his second missionary journey (Acts 18:1).
46.contexte:
Corinth is a large, cosmopolitan port city, wealthy and known for its debauchery. The Church Paul planted there is vibrant and full of spiritual gifts, but also divided and proud. News brought by Chloe's household (1 Corinthians 1:11) and a letter of questions move Paul to write.

He responds point by point: divisions, a case of immorality, lawsuits among believers, marriage, meat offered to idols, the Lord's Supper, spiritual gifts, and resurrection. At the heart of the letter stands the hymn to love—the greatest of all: without it, even the most spectacular gifts are nothing (1 Corinthians 13:2).
plan: Divisions and the Wisdom of the Cross
Freedom and Meat Offered to Idols
themes: La prédication de la croix est une folie pour le monde, mais une puissance de Dieu (1 Corinthiens 1:18).
Beaucoup de membres, un seul corps (1 Corinthiens 12:12).
La foi, l'espérance et la charité demeurent ; la plus grande, c'est la charité (1 Corinthiens 13:13).
Si Christ n'est pas ressuscité, notre foi est vaine (1 Corinthiens 15:17).

versets.t: For the message of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God.

No temptation has overtaken you except what is common to mankind. And God is faithful; he will not let you be tempted beyond what you can bear. But when you are tempted, he will also provide a way out so that you can endure it.
And now these three remain: faith, hope and love. But the greatest of these is love.

For what I received I passed on to you as of first importance: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures…

46.christ: Paul is determined to know nothing among the Corinthians "except Jesus Christ and him crucified" (1 Corinthians 2:2). Chapter 15 preserves the earliest summary of the Gospel: Christ died for our sins, he was buried, he was raised on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3-4).

47.accroche: My grace is sufficient for you
47.resume: Paul's most personal letter. Contested in Corinth, he opens his heart: his sufferings, his weaknesses, his joy in reconciliation, and the discovery that God's power is perfected in weakness.
47.date: Around 56 A.D., from Macedonia, after the arrival of Titus (2 Corinthians 7:6).
47.destinataires: The Church of Corinth and all the Christians of Achaia.
47.contexte:
Between the two letters, relations have become strained. Paul made a painful visit to Corinth, then wrote a letter "with many tears" (2 Corinthians 2:4). Brilliant preachers, whom Paul calls ironically "these super-apostles" (2 Corinthians 11:5), challenge his authority. When Titus joins him in Macedonia with good news, Paul is relieved and writes.

He speaks of his sufferings, his weaknesses, of a "thorn in my flesh." And he reports the Lord's answer: "My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness" (2 Corinthians 12:9). In the middle of the letter, he also encourages generosity toward the poor Christians in Jerusalem.
themes: Consolés par Dieu pour pouvoir consoler les autres (2 Corinthiens 1:4).
Dieu aime celui qui donne avec joie (2 Corinthiens 9:7).
La puissance de Dieu se déploie dans nos limites (2 Corinthiens 12:9).

versets.t: But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellence of the power may be of God and not of us.
Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation; old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new.
So let each one give as he purposes in his heart, not grudgingly or of necessity; for God loves a cheerful giver.

And He said to me, "My grace is sufficient for you, for My strength is made perfect in weakness." Therefore most gladly I will rather boast in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me.

47.christ: Paul summarizes the work of Christ: "He made Him who knew no sin to be sin for us, that we might become the righteousness of God in Him" (2 Corinthians 5:21). And He became poor so that we might be enriched (2 Corinthians 8:9).

48.resume: Some preachers want to impose the Law of Moses on non-Jewish Christians. Paul responds with vigor: we are justified by faith in Christ alone, and called to live free, led by the Spirit.
48.date: Debated: around 48–49 A.D., just before the Jerusalem Council, or around 53–57 A.D.
48.destinataires: The churches of Galatia, probably those founded during the first journey (Antioch of Pisidia, Iconium, Lystra, Derbe).
48.contexte:
After Paul's departure, preachers from Judea taught the Galatians that they must be circumcised and observe the Law of Moses to be fully saved. Paul responds with rare vigor: there is no other gospel (Galatians 1:7). He even skips the thanksgiving that usually opens his letters.

He recalls his own journey, his confrontation with Peter at Antioch, and the example of Abraham, who was declared righteous by faith long before the law came. Christ has freed us for freedom (Galatians 5:1)—not to live according to the flesh, but to walk according to the Spirit, whose fruit is love, joy, peace (Galatians 5:22).
plan: Freedom and Life by the Spirit
themes: L'homme est justifié par la foi en Jésus-Christ, non par les œuvres de la loi (Galates 2:16).
Dieu a envoyé dans nos cœurs l'Esprit qui crie : Abba ! Père ! (Galates 4:6)
C'est pour la liberté que Christ nous a affranchis (Galates 5:1).
Une vie nouvelle produite par l'Esprit (Galates 5:22-23).

versets.t: I have been crucified with Christ; and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me; and the life which I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave Himself up for me.
It was for freedom that Christ set us free; therefore keep standing firm and do not be subject again to a yoke of slavery.
But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control; against such things there is no law.

48.christ: "I have been crucified with Christ; and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me" (Galatians 2:20). For Paul, to claim that we gain righteousness through the law is to say that Christ died in vain (Galatians 2:21).

49.accroche: Saved by Grace, United in Christ
49.resume: A contemplation of God's eternal plan: chosen, adopted, saved by grace, Jews and Gentiles brought together in one body. Then the call to live in a manner worthy of that calling, even in spiritual warfare.
49.auteur: L'apôtre Paul (Éphésiens 1:1), alors prisonnier (Éphésiens 4:1). Certains spécialistes y voient l'œuvre d'un disciple de Paul.
49.date: Around 60–62 AD, during Paul's imprisonment, probably in Rome. The letter is delivered by Tychicus (Ephesians 6:21).
49.destinataires: The Christians at Ephesus, where Paul had spent three years (Acts 20:31). Several ancient manuscripts don't include the phrase
49.contexte:
Ephesians doesn't respond to a crisis—it's a hymn of praise. The first half unfolds God's plan: we have been chosen, adopted, redeemed in Christ; saved by grace through faith, not by works (Ephesians 2:8–9); Jews and Gentiles are brought together in one body, the wall of separation is torn down.

The second half draws out the implications: walk in a manner worthy of that calling, in unity, purity, and love, in marriage, family, and work. The letter closes with the armor of God, to stand firm against the schemes of the devil (Ephesians 6:11).
plan: Saved by Grace, United in One Body
themes: Le salut est un don de Dieu, reçu par la foi (Éphésiens 2:8).
Juifs et païens forment un seul peuple (Éphésiens 2:14).
Conserver l'unité de l'esprit par le lien de la paix (Éphésiens 4:3).
Se fortifier dans le Seigneur et revêtir les armes de Dieu (Éphésiens 6:10-11).

versets.t: For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast.
Be kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you.
Finally, be strong in the Lord and in the strength of his might.

50.accroche: Joy in the Midst of Chains
50.resume: A prisoner, Paul writes to a church he loves to thank them for their support. His letter breathes joy and calls for humility by following Christ, who humbled himself even to the cross.
50.auteur: L'apôtre Paul, avec Timothée (Philippiens 1:1), alors dans les liens (Philippiens 1:13).
50.date: Around 61–62 AD, likely written from Rome.
50.destinataires: The church at Philippi, the first church founded in Europe (Acts 16:12), which faithfully supported Paul.
50.contexte:
Paul is in prison and doesn't know if he will come out alive. The Philippians sent him a gift through Epaphroditus, who became gravely ill and nearly died (Philippians 2:27). Paul thanks them, reassures them, and encourages them.

The word "joy" runs throughout the letter, despite the chains: "Rejoice in the Lord always. Again I will say, rejoice!" (Philippians 4:4). Paul calls the church to unity and humility, following the example of Christ who emptied himself. He also urges two women in the church, Euodia and Syntyche, to be reconciled.
plan: The joy and peace of God
themes: Une joie qui ne dépend pas des circonstances (Philippiens 4:4).
Avoir les mêmes sentiments que le Christ (Philippiens 2:5).
J'ai appris à être content de l'état où je me trouve (Philippiens 4:11).
La paix de Dieu garde les cœurs de ceux qui prient (Philippiens 4:6-7).

versets.t: For to me, to live is Christ, and to die is gain.
Rejoice in the Lord always. Again I will say, rejoice!

Be anxious for nothing, but in everything by prayer and supplication, with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God; and the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus.
I can do all things through Christ who strengthens me.

50.christ: The hymn in Philippians 2 tells the journey of Christ: from divine nature, he emptied himself, became a servant, obedient even to death on a cross; therefore God has highly exalted him, "that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow" (Philippians 2:10).

51.resume: Facing a blend of religious practices and "philosophy," Paul demonstrates the greatness of Christ: in him dwells all the fullness of God. Whoever has him needs nothing else.
51.auteur: L'apôtre Paul, avec Timothée (Colossiens 1:1), alors prisonnier (Colossiens 4:18).
51.date: Around 60-62 A.D., written at the same time as the letter to Philemon; it was delivered by Tychicus and Onesimus (Colossians 4:7-9).
51.destinataires: The Church of Colossae, in Phrygia, founded by Epaphras (Colossians 1:7). Paul had never visited it.
51.contexte:
Teachers there were mixing Christian faith with Jewish practices, ascetic rules, the worship of angels, and a supposed "philosophy" (Colossians 2:8). Paul responds by showing the supremacy of Christ: everything was created by him and for him, and "in him dwells all the fullness of the Godhead bodily" (Colossians 2:9).

If Christ is everything, you need nothing else to be complete. Paul draws out the consequences for daily life: seek the things above, put off the old self, put on love, and do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus (Colossians 3:17).
plan: Fullness in Christ Against False Doctrines
themes: Il est l'image du Dieu invisible, et tout subsiste en lui (Colossiens 1:15).
En Christ, nous avons tout pleinement (Colossiens 2:10).
Faire tout de bon cœur, comme pour le Seigneur (Colossiens 3:23).

versets.t: For in him dwells all the fullness of the Godhead bodily.
Set your mind on things above, not on things on the earth.
And whatever you do, in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks through him to God the Father.
Whatever you do, do it wholeheartedly, as working for the Lord and not for human masters…

51.christ: Colossians contains one of the most beautiful hymns to Christ: he is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation; all things were created through him and for him, and in him all things hold together (Colossians 1:15-17).

52.resume: Driven from Thessalonica after just a few weeks, Paul encourages this young persecuted church. He answers their anxiety about believers who have died: they will be raised when the Lord returns.
52.auteur: L'apôtre Paul, avec Silvain (Silas) et Timothée (1 Thessaloniciens 1:1).
52.date: Around A.D. 50–51, written from Corinth. This is one of Paul's earliest letters, possibly the oldest writing in the New Testament.
52.destinataires: The Church of Thessalonica, in Macedonia, founded during his second missionary journey (Acts 17:1).
52.contexte:
Paul was forced to leave Thessalonica hurriedly under pressure from his opponents. Concerned for this young and persecuted church, he sends Timothy, who returns with good news of their faith and love (1 Thessalonians 3:6). Paul writes to encourage them.

One question troubles them: what will happen to believers who die before the Lord's return? Paul answers: the dead in Christ will rise first, then we will all be caught up together with the Lord (1 Thessalonians 4:16–17). He urges them to live holy lives, to work diligently, and not to grieve like those who have no hope.
plan: Paul's Ministry and Timothy's Good News
A Holy Life and the Lord's Return
themes: La mort n'a pas le dernier mot pour ceux qui sont en Christ (1 Thessaloniciens 4:14).
Ce que Dieu veut, c'est votre sanctification (1 Thessaloniciens 4:3).
Il viendra comme un voleur dans la nuit : restons éveillés (1 Thessaloniciens 5:2).
Soyez toujours joyeux, priez sans cesse (1 Thessaloniciens 5:16-17).

versets.t: For the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trumpet of God. And the dead in Christ will rise first. Then we who are alive and remain will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air. And thus we will always be with the Lord.
Rejoice always. Pray without ceasing. In everything give thanks, for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for you.

52.christ: the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trumpet of God

53.resume: A few months later, a rumor spreads that the day of the Lord has already come. Paul reassures the persecuted, clears up the confusion, and confronts those who have stopped working.
53.auteur: L'apôtre Paul, avec Silvain et Timothée (2 Thessaloniciens 1:1).
53.date: Shortly after the first letter, around AD 51.
53.contexte:
Persecution continues, and confusion has arisen: some claim, perhaps through a letter attributed to Paul, that the day of the Lord has already come (2 Thessalonians 2:2). The result: anxiety, and in some cases laziness—why work if the end is imminent?

Paul reassures them: other events must come first, notably the appearance of "the man of lawlessness" (2 Thessalonians 2:3). He encourages the persecuted by reminding them of God's justice, and he is firm with those living in disorder: "If anyone is not willing to work, then he is not to eat, either" (2 Thessalonians 3:10).
plan: The day of the Lord has not yet come
themes: Ne vous lassez pas de faire le bien (2 Thessaloniciens 3:13).
Le Seigneur Jésus apparaîtra du ciel (2 Thessaloniciens 1:7).
Attendre le Seigneur n'est pas une excuse pour la paresse (2 Thessaloniciens 3:10).
Le Seigneur est fidèle, il vous affermira (2 Thessaloniciens 3:3).

versets.t: The Lord is faithful, and he will strengthen you and guard you from the evil one.
As for you, brothers, do not grow weary in doing what is good.

53.christ: The Lord Jesus will appear from heaven with his mighty angels (2 Thessalonians 1:7), and he will destroy the lawless one by the brightness of his coming (2 Thessalonians 2:8). In the meantime: "The Lord is faithful, and he will strengthen you and guard you from the evil one" (2 Thessalonians 3:3).

54.resume: Paul writes to his spiritual son Timothy, left in Ephesus to counter false teachings. He gives him a guide for the life of the Church: prayer, leaders, widows, money, and the good fight of faith.
54.auteur: L'apôtre Paul (1 Timothée 1:1). Avec 2 Timothée et Tite, on l'appelle « épître pastorale ». Beaucoup de spécialistes modernes y voient l'œuvre d'un disciple de Paul ; l'Église l'a reçue comme une lettre de l'apôtre.
54.date: Around 62–64 AD, after Paul's first Roman imprisonment.
54.destinataires: Timothy, whom Paul had asked to remain in Ephesus (1 Timothy 1:3).
54.contexte:
Timothy is Paul's spiritual son, a relatively young and reserved leader. Paul left him in Ephesus to set the Church in order, where some are devoted to fables and endless genealogies (1 Timothy 1:4).

The letter is a guide for the life of the Church: prayer for authorities, the qualities expected of elders and deacons, care for widows, the danger of the love of money. Paul also encourages Timothy personally: "Let no one despise your youth; but be an example to the believers" (1 Timothy 4:12).
plan: A Good Servant of Jesus Christ
Money and the Good Fight of Faith
themes: Garder l'enseignement fidèle face aux fables (1 Timothée 1:3-4).
Le caractère compte plus que le talent (1 Timothée 3:2).
La piété avec le contentement est une grande source de gain (1 Timothée 6:6).
Combats le bon combat de la foi (1 Timothée 6:12).

versets.t: This is a faithful saying and worthy of all acceptance, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am chief.
For there is one God and one Mediator between God and men, the Man Christ Jesus, who gave Himself a ransom for all, to be testified in due time…
Let no one despise your youth; but be an example to the believers in word, in conduct, in love, in spirit, in faith, in purity.
Fight the good fight of faith, lay hold on eternal life, to which you were also called and have confessed the good confession in the presence of many witnesses.

54.christ: "Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am chief" (1 Timothy 1:15). He is the one Mediator between God and men, who gave Himself a ransom for all (1 Timothy 2:5–6).

55.resume: Paul's final letter, written from prison in Rome shortly before his death. He passes the torch to Timothy: do not be ashamed of the Gospel, pass it on, remain committed to Scripture, preach the Word.
55.auteur: L'apôtre Paul (2 Timothée 1:1), dans sa dernière captivité.
55.date: Around 64–67 A.D., from Rome, shortly before Paul's martyrdom.
55.contexte:
Paul is imprisoned in Rome again, under harsh conditions. Nearly everyone has abandoned him: "Only Luke is with me" (2 Timothy 4:11). He knows his end is near: "I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith" (2 Timothy 4:7).

He passes the torch to Timothy: do not be ashamed of the Gospel, suffer with him, entrust the teaching to faithful men, remain committed to Scripture inspired by God. He also asks Timothy to come quickly, bringing the cloak left at Troas and his books (2 Timothy 4:13)—a deeply human detail in the apostle's final letter.
plan: Do Not Be Ashamed of the Gospel
themes: Dieu ne nous a pas donné un esprit de timidité (2 Timothée 1:7).
Confier l'enseignement à des hommes fidèles, capables d'enseigner à d'autres (2 Timothée 2:2).
Toute Écriture est inspirée de Dieu (2 Timothée 3:16).
Garder la foi jusqu'au bout (2 Timothée 4:7).

versets.t: For God has not given us a spirit of fear, but of power and of love and of a sound mind.
And the things that you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit these to faithful men who will be able to teach others also.

All Scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness, that the man of God may be complete, thoroughly equipped for every good work.
I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith.

55.christ: Paul reminds us of what matters: "Remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, descended from David" (2 Timothy 2:8). Our Savior Jesus Christ has destroyed death and brought life and immortality to light through the Gospel (2 Timothy 1:10).

56.resume: Paul writes to Titus, left in Crete to organize the churches. Sound doctrine must produce a beautiful life: God's grace teaches us to live with wisdom, justice, and godliness.
56.auteur: L'apôtre Paul (Tite 1:1). Comme pour les lettres à Timothée, son attribution est discutée par une partie des spécialistes modernes.
56.date: Around AD 62–64, at the same time as 1 Timothy.
56.destinataires: Titus, Paul's collaborator of Greek origin, left in Crete (Titus 1:5).
56.contexte:
Titus accompanied Paul on several occasions and was entrusted with delicate missions, notably in Corinth. Paul left him in Crete to put the churches in order and appoint elders in each city (Titus 1:5). The task is not simple: false teachers are causing trouble there.

The letter emphasizes a connection: sound doctrine produces a beautiful life. Leaders must be blameless, and each group of believers—the elderly, the young, servants—is called to honor the Gospel through their conduct. For God's grace, the source of salvation, teaches us to live according to wisdom, justice, and godliness (Titus 2:11–12).
themes: Ce qu'on croit se voit dans la manière de vivre (Tite 2:1).
La grâce nous apprend à vivre autrement (Tite 2:12).
Sauvés par la miséricorde de Dieu et le renouvellement du Saint-Esprit (Tite 3:5).
Les croyants sont appelés à s'appliquer aux bonnes œuvres (Tite 3:8).

versets.t: For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation for all people. It teaches us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions, and to live self-controlled, upright, and godly lives in the present age…
He saved us, not because of righteous things we had done, but because of his mercy. He saved us through the washing of rebirth and renewal by the Holy Spirit…

57.resume: A tactful letter: Paul returns to his master Philemon the runaway slave Onesimus, who has become a Christian, and asks him to welcome him as a beloved brother.
57.date: Around 60-62 A.D., at the same time as the letter to the Colossians.
57.destinataires: Philemon, a Christian in Colossae in whose home the church gathered, as well as Apphia and Archippus (Philemon 1:2).
57.contexte:
Onesimus, Philemon's slave, had run away, perhaps after wronging his master. He met Paul in prison and became a Christian. Paul sends him back to Philemon with this letter, a short plea full of affection.

He asks Philemon to welcome Onesimus "no longer as a slave, but as more than a slave, as a beloved brother" (Philemon 1:16), and offers to pay himself what he might owe. The name Onesimus means "useful," and Paul plays on this word: once useless, he is now useful (Philemon 1:11).
themes: En Christ, le maître et l'esclave deviennent frères (Philémon 1:16).
Paul se met entre les deux pour les réconcilier (Philémon 1:18).

versets.t: I pray that the sharing of your faith may become effective through the knowledge of every good thing which is in you for Christ's sake.
no longer as a slave, but more than a slave, a beloved brother—especially to me, but how much more to you, both in the flesh and in the Lord.

57.christ: Paul writes: "If he has wronged you or owes you anything, charge that to my account" (Philemon 1:18). This is the very image of what Christ has done for us: He took our debt upon Himself to reconcile us with the Father.

58.resume: To Jewish Christians tempted to turn back, the author shows that Jesus is superior to the angels, to Moses, and to Aaron's priesthood. His unique sacrifice opens a new covenant: hold firm in your faith.
58.auteur: Inconnu. On a proposé Paul, Barnabas, Apollos… Au IIIe siècle déjà, Origène estimait que Dieu seul sait qui a écrit cette lettre.
58.date: Probably before 70 AD: the temple sacrifices are described as still being offered (Hebrews 10:11).
58.destinataires: Jewish Christians who are suffering persecution and tempted to return to the old worship.
58.contexte:
The recipients have already suffered for their faith (Hebrews 10:32), but they are growing discouraged. Some are tempted to turn back to temple worship and the sacrifices they knew. The author shows them that this would be trading reality for its shadow.

Jesus is superior to the angels, to Moses, to Joshua, to Aaron's priesthood; he is the High Priest according to the order of Melchizedek, who offered one unique and perfect sacrifice. The letter presents a gallery of heroes of faith, from Abel to the prophets, and calls you to run with perseverance, "fixing your eyes on Jesus" (Hebrews 12:2).
plan: The New Covenant and the Perfect Sacrifice
themes: Dieu nous a parlé par le Fils (Hébreux 1:2).
Un souverain sacrificateur qui compatit à nos faiblesses (Hébreux 4:15).
Une ferme assurance des choses qu'on espère (Hébreux 11:1).
Courir avec persévérance, les regards sur Jésus (Hébreux 12:1-2).

versets.t: For the word of God is living and active, sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing to the division of soul and of spirit, of joints and of marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart.

For we do not have a High Priest who cannot sympathize with our weaknesses, but was in all points tempted as we are, yet without sin. Let us therefore come boldly to the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy and find grace to help in time of need.
Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen.
Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever.

58.christ: The entire letter is centered on Christ: after speaking through the prophets, God "has spoken to us by His Son" (Hebrews 1:2). He is the perfect High Priest, and "Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever" (Hebrews 13:8).

59.resume: A letter of practical wisdom, in line with Proverbs and the Sermon on the Mount: trials, the tongue, the rich and the poor, prayer. Faith without works is dead.
59.auteur: « Jacques, serviteur de Dieu et du Seigneur Jésus-Christ » (Jacques 1:1) ; la tradition l'identifie à Jacques, frère du Seigneur et responsable de l'Église de Jérusalem.
59.date: Possibly around AD 45-50, which would make it one of the earliest writings of the New Testament; in any case before James's death in AD 62.
59.destinataires: "To the twelve tribes scattered abroad" (James 1:1): Jewish Christian believers dispersed outside Judea.
59.contexte:
James, the brother of Jesus, did not believe in him during his ministry (John 7:5); the risen Christ appeared to him (1 Corinthians 15:7), and he became one of the pillars of the Jerusalem church. His letter reads like a collection of wisdom.

He speaks of trials, the tongue, wealth and poverty, prayer. His central message: faith that produces no works is a dead faith (James 2:17). He does not contradict Paul: Paul fights against the idea that you could earn your salvation by your works; James fights against a faith that changes nothing in your life.
themes: L'épreuve de la foi produit la patience (Jacques 1:2-3).
Ne pas se contenter d'écouter la Parole (Jacques 1:22).
Une petite flamme qui peut embraser une grande forêt (Jacques 3:5).
La prière fervente du juste a une grande efficacité (Jacques 5:16).

versets.t: If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask of God, who gives to all liberally and without reproach, and it will be given to him.
But be doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving yourselves with false reasoning.
Thus also faith by itself, if it does not have works, is dead.
Confess your trespasses to one another, and pray for one another, that you may be healed. The effective, fervent prayer of a righteous man avails much.

59.christ: James rarely uses the name of Jesus, but his letter is steeped in his teaching, echoing the Sermon on the Mount. He calls him "our glorious Lord Jesus Christ" (James 2:1) and awaits his coming (James 5:8).

60.resume: To Christians despised and mistreated for their faith, Peter reminds them of their living hope and their identity as God's people, and calls them to suffer for what is right by following in Christ's footsteps.
60.auteur: L'apôtre Pierre (1 Pierre 1:1), avec l'aide de Silvain (1 Pierre 5:12).
60.destinataires: Christians scattered throughout Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia (1 Peter 1:1), in Asia Minor.
plan: A Holy People Among the Nations
themes: Régénérés pour une espérance vivante par la résurrection de Jésus (1 Pierre 1:3).
Un sacerdoce royal, une nation sainte (1 Pierre 2:9).
Souffrir pour avoir fait le bien, comme le Christ (1 Pierre 3:17).
Déchargez-vous sur lui de tous vos soucis (1 Pierre 5:7).

versets.t: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who according to His great mercy has caused us to be born again to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead…
But you are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, His own special people, that you may proclaim the praises of Him who called you out of darkness into His marvelous light…
But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts, and always be ready to give a defense to everyone who asks you a reason for the hope that is in you, with meekness and fear…
casting all your care upon Him, for He cares for you.

60.christ: Peter witnessed his Master's suffering. He writes: Christ

61.resume: Sensing his death is near, Peter calls believers to grow in faith, to hold fast to inspired Scripture, to guard themselves against false teachers, and to await the Lord's day, which is surely coming.
61.auteur: Elle se présente comme une lettre de Simon Pierre (2 Pierre 1:1), témoin de la transfiguration (2 Pierre 1:16). Son attribution a été discutée dès l'Antiquité.
61.date: Shortly before Peter's death (2 Peter 1:14), around AD 64–67
61.destinataires: The same readers as his first letter (2 Peter 3:1).
61.contexte:
Peter knows his death is near. He writes to remind them of what matters most: add to your faith virtue, knowledge, patience, love; remain attached to the prophetic word, for it was men moved by the Holy Spirit who spoke from God (2 Peter 1:21). For false teachers have slipped in, who despise all authority.

Some even mock the Lord's return: nothing has changed since creation! Peter answers that to the Lord, a day is like a thousand years; if He delays, it is because He is patient and wants everyone to come to repentance (2 Peter 3:9).
themes: Croissez dans la grâce et dans la connaissance de Jésus-Christ (2 Pierre 3:18).
Des hommes poussés par l'Esprit ont parlé de la part de Dieu (2 Pierre 1:21).
Il veut que tous arrivent à la repentance (2 Pierre 3:9).
De nouveaux cieux et une nouvelle terre, où la justice habitera (2 Pierre 3:13).

versets.t: For prophecy never came by the will of man, but holy men of God spoke as they were moved by the Holy Spirit.
The Lord is not slack concerning His promise, as some count slackness, but is longsuffering toward us, not willing that any should perish but that all should come to repentance.
But grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. To Him be the glory both now and forever. Amen.

62.resume: After a group denying that Jesus is the Christ come in the flesh departs, John gives believers markers to know they have eternal life: believe, obey, love.
62.auteur: La lettre n'est pas signée, mais son vocabulaire est très proche de l'Évangile de Jean ; la tradition l'attribue à l'apôtre Jean. L'auteur se présente comme témoin direct de Jésus (1 Jean 1:1).
62.contexte:
A group has left the community: "they went out from us, but they were not of us" (1 John 2:19). These people claim to know God, but deny that Jesus is the Christ come in the flesh, and care neither about sin nor about brotherly love. Those who remain are troubled: are we really in the truth?

John gives them markers for assurance: believe that Jesus is the Christ come in the flesh, keep his commandments, love your brothers. "God is love" (1 John 4:8). He writes so that they may know they have eternal life (1 John 5:13).
plan: Children of God: Let Us Love One Another
The Victory of Faith and Assurance
themes: Dieu est lumière : marcher avec lui, c'est sortir des ténèbres (1 Jean 1:5).
Si nous confessons nos péchés, il est fidèle et juste pour nous pardonner (1 Jean 1:9).
Nous l'aimons parce qu'il nous a aimés le premier (1 Jean 4:19).
Savoir que l'on a la vie éternelle (1 Jean 5:13).

versets.t: If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
Behold, what manner of love the Father hath bestowed upon us, that we should be called the sons of God! And that is what we are. Therefore the world does not know us, because it did not know Him.
We love Him because He first loved us.
These things I have written to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, that you may know that you have eternal life.

62.christ: John heard, saw, beheld, and touched the Word of life (1 John 1:1). Jesus Christ the righteous is our advocate with the Father and the atoning sacrifice for our sins (1 John 2:1–2); in Him, God has manifested His love (1 John 4:9).

63.resume: A short letter from "the elder": walk in love, which means obeying God's commandments, and do not receive those who deny that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh.
63.auteur: « L'ancien » (2 Jean 1:1), que la tradition identifie à l'apôtre Jean.
63.date: Around 85–95 AD, at the same time as the first letter.
63.destinataires: The letter is addressed "to the elect lady and her children" (2 John 1:1): either a Christian woman and her family, or a local church described in figurative language.
63.contexte:
Itinerant preachers are traveling from church to church, and some are teaching that Jesus Christ did not come in the flesh (2 John 1:7). John writes to give a warning: walk in love, which means living according to God's commandments, and do not receive in your home those who bring another doctrine (2 John 1:10).

The letter shows that truth and love go together: love without truth becomes indulgence, truth without love becomes harshness.
themes: L'amour consiste à marcher selon ses commandements (2 Jean 1:6).
Tout enseignement doit confesser que Jésus-Christ est venu en chair (2 Jean 1:7).

versets.t: And love consists in walking according to His commandments. This is the commandment in which you must walk, as you learned from the beginning.

63.christ: The criterion is clear: to confess that "Jesus Christ has come in the flesh" (2 John 1:7). He who abides in the doctrine of Christ has both the Father and the Son (2 John 1:9).

64.resume: John commends Gaius for his hospitality toward traveling missionaries, denounces the pride of Diotrephes, and recommends Demetrius.
64.auteur: « L'ancien » (3 Jean 1:1), que la tradition identifie à l'apôtre Jean.
64.destinataires: Gaius, "the beloved" (3 John 1:1), a member of a church in Asia Minor.
64.contexte:
John commends Gaius for welcoming traveling missionary brothers, even those he doesn't know (3 John 1:5). He denounces Diotrephes, however, "who loves to have the preeminence," refuses John's authority, and expels from the church those who receive these brothers (3 John 1:9–10). He finally recommends Demetrius, who has a good testimony.

This brief letter offers a glimpse into the life of the early churches: hospitality toward missionaries was vital, and the pride of a single leader could shut everything down.
themes: Accueillir ceux qui servent, c'est travailler avec eux (3 Jean 1:8).
L'orgueil d'aimer être le premier abîme l'Église (3 Jean 1:9).
Celui qui fait le bien est de Dieu (3 Jean 1:11).

versets.t: Beloved, do not imitate what is evil, but what is good. He who does good is of God, but he who does evil has not seen God.

64.christ: The missionaries whom Gaius welcomes have gone out "for the sake of the Name" (3 John 1:7). To support them is to become "fellow workers for the truth" (3 John 1:8).

65.resume: Ungodly people have crept into the Church and are turning grace into an excuse for disorder. Jude calls believers to fight for the faith that was delivered to the saints once for all, and concludes with a magnificent doxology.
65.auteur: « Jude, serviteur de Jésus-Christ, et frère de Jacques » (Jude 1:1), traditionnellement l'un des frères de Jésus (Matthieu 13:55).
65.date: Probably between 65 and 80 A.D. The letter shares many similarities with 2 Peter.
65.destinataires: Christians called by God, loved by God the Father, and kept for Jesus Christ (Jude 1:1).
65.contexte:
Jude intended to write about the common salvation, but he must change his subject: ungodly people have crept into the Church, "who change the grace of our God into lewdness" (Jude 1:4). He calls believers "to contend earnestly for the faith which was once for all delivered to the saints" (Jude 1:3).

He reminds them of examples of judgment—Israel in the wilderness, the fallen angels, Sodom, Cain, Balaam, Korah—and even quotes a prophecy attributed to Enoch (Jude 1:14). The letter ends with one of the most beautiful doxologies in the Bible: to Him who is able to keep you from stumbling (Jude 1:24).
plan: Keep Yourselves in the Love of God
themes: Une foi reçue une fois pour toutes, à garder et à défendre (Jude 1:3).
La grâce n'est pas une permission de pécher (Jude 1:4).
Dieu peut nous garder de toute chute (Jude 1:24).

versets.t: But you, beloved, building yourselves up on your most holy faith, praying in the Holy Spirit, keep yourselves in the love of God, looking for the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ unto eternal life.

Now to Him who is able to keep you from stumbling, and to present you faultless before the presence of His glory with exceeding joy, to God our Savior, who alone is wise, be glory and majesty, dominion and power, both now and forever. Amen.

65.christ: The letter opens and closes on God's faithfulness: believers are "kept for Jesus Christ" (Jude 1:1), and God, our Savior, is able to present them before His glory "faultless and with exceeding joy" (Jude 1:24).

66.resume: Exiled on Patmos, John receives a revelation of the glorified Christ: letters to seven churches, then visions of the battle between God and the powers of evil, culminating in the victory of the Lamb and the new Jerusalem.
66.auteur: Jean (Apocalypse 1:9), que la tradition identifie à l'apôtre Jean.
66.date: Around 95 AD, under Emperor Domitian, according to the testimony of Irenaeus in the second century.
66.destinataires: Seven churches in the province of Asia, in Asia Minor (Revelation 1:4), and through them the whole Church.
66.contexte:
John is exiled on the island of Patmos, "because of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus" (Revelation 1:9). On the Lord's Day, he receives a revelation—this is what the Greek word "apocalypse" means. The glorified Christ first dictates to him seven letters to seven churches, with commendations and rebukes.

Then John is transported before God's throne. A series of visions—seals, trumpets, bowls—describe the battle between God and the powers of evil, expressed in symbolic language rooted in the Old Testament. Interpretations differ on the details, but the message is clear: the Lamb has overcome. The book ends with new heavens and a new earth, where God will wipe away every tear (Revelation 21:4).
plan: The Vision of the Glorified Christ
The Letters to the Seven Churches
The Bowls and the Fall of Babylon
The Return of Christ and Judgment
themes: Le trône de Dieu domine toute l'histoire (Apocalypse 4:2).
Le Lion de Juda est un Agneau immolé, et il a vaincu (Apocalypse 5:5-6).

versets.t: "I am the Alpha and the Omega," says the Lord God, "who is, and who was, and who is to come, the Almighty."
Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears My voice and opens the door, I will come in to him and dine with him, and he with Me.
And God will wipe away every tear from their eyes; there shall be no more death, nor sorrow, nor crying. There shall be no more pain, for the former things have passed away.
He who testifies to these things says, "Surely I am coming quickly." Amen. Even so, come, Lord Jesus!

66.christ: Revelation is the "Revelation of Jesus Christ" (Revelation 1:1). He appears here as the Alpha and the Omega, the Lion of the tribe of Judah who is revealed to be a slain Lamb (Revelation 5:5-6), the King of kings who returns. The Bible closes with His promise: "Surely I am coming quickly" (Revelation 22:20).
